nameStory: Common mallow earned its name from being the most widespread member of the mallow family, found growing 'commonly' in gardens, fields, and waste places across Europe before spreading worldwide. The word 'mallow' comes from the Old English 'malwe,' which traces back to the Latin 'malva,' referring to the soft, mucilaginous texture of the plant's leaves and stems.
description: Common mallow is a robust, upright wildflower that can grow 3-4 feet tall with a bushy, spreading habit. It's easily recognized by its showy purple-pink flowers with darker purple veins that look like delicate watercolor paintings. The plant has a vigorous, almost weedy nature and produces rounded, lobed leaves that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch. Originally from Europe, it has made itself at home in New England's disturbed soils and sunny spots.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright mauve-purple flowers about 1-2 inches across with five petals marked by distinctive dark purple veins that radiate from the center like painted lines

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Round to kidney-shaped leaves with 5-7 shallow lobes, feeling soft and slightly velvety with a pleasant, mild green smell when crushed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright plant reaching 3-4 feet with multiple branching stems that feel slightly sticky and have a succulent-like thickness

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Distinctive round, flat seed pods that split into wedge-shaped sections, often called 'cheeses' because they resemble small wheels of cheese

habitat: Look for common mallow in disturbed soils like roadsides, vacant lots, garden edges, and old fields throughout New England's lower elevations. It thrives in sunny spots with rich, well-drained soil and often appears where the ground has been recently disturbed. You'll frequently find it growing alongside other weedy species like dandelions and plantains in suburban and agricultural areas.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as soft, rounded rosettes close to the ground, with the distinctive lobed shape becoming apparent as they mature.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with showy purple flowers appearing continuously from June through August, making this the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall while the characteristic cheese-wheel seed pods develop and ripen, often persisting after flowers fade.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground as an annual or acts as a short-lived perennial, leaving behind dried seed pods that may remain visible.

funFact: The round, segmented seed pods of common mallow are completely edible and taste like mild nuts - they were actually eaten as snacks by children in Europe for centuries, earning the plant the nickname 'cheeses' because the seed pods look exactly like tiny wheels of cheese!
confusionNotes: Common mallow is most easily confused with its smaller cousin, dwarf mallow, but common mallow grows much taller (3-4 feet vs. low and sprawling) and has larger, more vibrant flowers. Remember: 'common' means tall and showy, while 'dwarf' stays low to the ground.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'common' mallow, this species is actually much less frequently encountered in New England than dwarf mallow, with only 16 recorded observations. The 'common' name refers to its status in its native European range, where it's the most typical mallow species.
compareHints: Common mallow stands out from other New England mallows by being the tallest and most robust, with the largest and most intensely colored flowers. While musk mallow has deeply cut, feathery leaves and dwarf mallow stays prostrate on the ground, common mallow combines upright growth with the simple, lobed leaves typical of the genus. Its flowers are also more richly colored than the pale pink blooms of most other local mallow species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's mallows, musk mallow stands out with its deeply-cut, narrow leaf segments - quite different from the broad, rounded leaves of common mallow or the small, kidney-shaped leaves of dwarf mallow.
Unlike its cousin musk mallow which grows upright with deeply divided leaves, dwarf mallow stays low and sprawling with round, shallowly-lobed leaves.

Among its mallow relatives, greater musk-mallow stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - they're cut almost to the midrib unlike the merely lobed leaves of common mallow or the heart-shaped leaves of dwarf mallow.
Unlike the perennial musk mallow with its deeply divided leaves and smaller flowers, Royal Mallow is an annual with simpler heart-shaped leaves and much larger blooms.
Among New England's mallows, cheeseweed mallow is distinguished by having the smallest flowers and the smoothest seed pods.
Eastern Tree-mallow stands out from other mallows in New England primarily by its exceptional height - it can reach 6 feet compared to the 1-3 feet typical of Musk Mallow or Common Mallow.
